q-129549:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant. 

Making a substitution $x+y=u,$ $\text{d}x=\text{d}u,$ we get.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{y}^{1+y}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[-\frac{1}{u}]}_{y}^{1+y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(-\frac{1}{y+1}+\frac{1}{y})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[\frac{1}{y}-\frac{1}{y+1}]\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}[\frac{1}{y}-\frac{1}{y+1}]\,\text{d}y & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡y-\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)]_{1}^{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{y}{y+1}){|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3}\cdot 2) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

q-72050:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:    

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{2}^{4}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{2}^{4}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}{[\frac{\,{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{256}{4}-\frac{16}{4})\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}60{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}60{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =60{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =60\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =20\end{aligned}
$$

q-72266:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:        

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{-2}^{2}9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{-2}^{2}9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}9{y}^{2}[{\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}9{y}^{2}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{-2}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}9{y}^{2}(\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-2)^{3}}{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}9{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{16}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}48{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}48{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =[16{y}^{3}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =16({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =16\cdot 2 \\  & =32\end{aligned}
$$

q-129568:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:   

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

Making a substitution $x+y=u,$ $\text{d}x=\text{d}u,$ we get.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[{\int }_{y}^{y+\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[\operatorname{sin}⁡u]_{y}^{y+\pi /4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡y]\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }[\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡y]\text{d}y & ={[\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+\frac{\pi }{4})]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4}))-(\operatorname{cos}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})) \\  & =(-1+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-(1-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}-2\end{aligned}
$$

q-129644:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{1}^{2}(x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\,{[xy+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[(2x+\frac{8}{3})-(x+\frac{1}{3})]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(x+\frac{7}{3})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(x+\frac{7}{3})\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{7x}{3}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{7}{3})-(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{7}{3}) \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-164350:
The full expression describing all points on our hyperbolic cylinder is

$$
\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{2}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{2}=1}.
$$

This is a hyperbola centered at $(-1,4).$

q-164416:
The full expression describing all points on our hyperbolic cylinder is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4}=1}.
$$

This is a hyperbola centered at $(0,-1).$

q-164401:
To find the trace in the $xz$-plane, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the cylinder, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{8}+\frac{(0-1)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-4)^{2}}{8}+\frac{1}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-4)^{2}}{8} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ (x-4)^{2} & =4 \\ x-4 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =4\pm 2 \\ x & =2,6\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of two lines $x=2$ and $x=6$ in the $xz$-plane.

q-164412:
To find the intersection of the cylinder and the plane $z=4,$ we substitute $z=4$ into the equation of the cylinder. However, since the equation has no (explicit) $z$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3(x+2)^{2} & =6(y+3) \\ (x+2)^{2} & =2(y+3) \\ (x+2)^{2} & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot (y+3).\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a parabola in the $xy$-plane with the vertex at $(-2,-3).$

q-164477:
Recall that the equation of an elliptic cylinder centered at $O$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

Thus, our equation is an elliptic cylinder with $a=b=\sqrt{2}.$

q-164479:
Recall that the equation of a hyperbolic cylinder, whose axis of symmetry is the $z$-axis, is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

Thus, our equation is a hyperbolic cylinder with $a=3,\,b=4.$

q-164510:
Recall that the equation of an elliptic paraboloid centered at $O$ whose axis of symmetry is the $z$-axis is given by

$$
z=\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

Thus, an elliptic paraboloid centered at $O$ whose axis of symmetry is the $x$**-axis** is given by

$$
x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, our equation is an elliptic paraboloid whose axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis and $b=\sqrt{2},\,c=2.$

q-164547:
Recall that the equation of a parabolic cylinder whose axis is the $z$-axis is given by

$$
{x}^{2}=4py.
$$

Thus, a parabolic cylinder whose axis is the $x$**-axis** is given by

$$
{y}^{2}=4pz.
$$

Therefore, our equation is a parabolic cylinder whose axis is the $x$-axis and $p=\frac{1}{2}.$

q-164554:
First, we complete the square in the $x$ and $z$ terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-4{z}^{2}-4x-y-16z-12 & =0 \\ 2({x}^{2}-2x)-4({z}^{2}+4z)-y-12 & =0 \\ 2[(x-1)^{2}-1]-4[(z+2)^{2}-4]-y-12 & =0 \\ 2(x-1)^{2}-2-4(z+2)^{2}+16-y-12 & =0 \\ 2(x-1)^{2}-4(z+2)^{2}-y+2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x-1)^{2}-4(z+2)^{2}-y+2 & =0 \\ 2(x-1)^{2}-4(z+2)^{2} & =y-2\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at $(1,2,-2).$

q-164550:
First, we complete the square in the $y$ and $z$ terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}-2y-8z-9 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-({y}^{2}+2y)+2({z}^{2}-4z)-9 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-(y+1)^{2}+1+2[(z-2)^{2}-4]-9 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-(y+1)^{2}+1+2(z-2)^{2}-8-9 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-(y+1)^{2}+2(z-2)^{2}-16 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-(y+1)^{2}+2(z-2)^{2}-16 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-(y+1)^{2}+2(z-2)^{2} & =16 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(z-2)^{2}}{8} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equation of a hyperboloid of one sheet centered at $(0,-1,2).$

q-129941:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{\sqrt{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\,{x}^{1/2}\,{y}^{1/2}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}})\text{ }(\sqrt{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y)\end{aligned}
$$
